Theme: _When the usual verb does not work_

== The entry

[quote]
____
some might be herding predators of themselves, needing to use a lure strategy rather than a chase strategy
____

== Intent — what is this actually asking?

Not what it would look like. What question about cognition, affect or conation
does trialling this answer? If the answer is "none", say so — that is a result.

The mockup has one affective channel doing all the work, and its sign is fixed.
Every brain fears the player: `CACSystem` raises `fear` for any entity within 30
units of the player, and `fearBias` (`src/components.js:40`) scales the magnitude
but never the direction (`src/systems.js:176-178`). Threat is therefore a
property of one entity — the player — and not of a pair of them.

That is what the entry puts pressure on. The cognitive question it forces is:
*is the affect an animal feels toward another entity a property of that entity,
or of the pair?* A cat approached by a hamster and a sheep approached by a
hamster cannot both produce fear, or there is nothing here. Answering "of the
pair" is a change of shape rather than a tuning exercise: the same approach by
the same herder comes to mean different things to different animals, for a
reason held in the animal.

The conative question is separate and sharper. There is exactly one compliance
mechanism — pressure — and every tool built on it (`BARK`, `CHAOS_BEAM`) is a
fear injector, so `FLEE` is the only route by which an animal ends up somewhere
the herder wanted it. So: can goal-arbitration reach the same displacement by an
appetitive route, and does the animal's behaviour distinguish the two?

It can, and one observable tells them apart honestly: *what happens when the
herder disengages*. Under pressure, an animal's motion is a function of the
herder's continued presence — stop, and it stops. Under an appetitive goal, the
motion is a function of the animal's own belief about a target, and it continues
after the herder stops. If that difference is not visible on screen, then
whatever has been built is pressure wearing different paint, and this document
has delivered nothing.

Underneath both sits an affective question: an affect that is not fear has to be
able to drive locomotion. `curiosity` exists and drives `INVESTIGATE` at gain 0.5
against `FLEE`'s 1.5 (`src/systems.js:214-226`), which is decorative; `trust`
(`src/components.js:44`) is declared and never read or written by any system.

== Logic — how would it work

The rule, stated so it could be implemented twice and agree. Name what is
observed, what is believed, what is chosen, and by whom.

What follows is *one rendering* of the entry, written so it can be built and
checked. It is not offered as what the entry means. Rejecting this formalisation
does not require rejecting the entry — if the rule below is wrong, the rule is
wrong, and the quote above is untouched by that.

=== R1 — the relation, and the one thing the model lacks

`stance(observerKind, otherKind) -> {PREDATOR_OF_ME, PEER, PREY_OF_ME}`

Directional and asymmetric. `stance(CAT, HAMSTER) = PREY_OF_ME` while
`stance(HAMSTER, CAT) = PREDATOR_OF_ME`. Today the mockup has no such relation:
threat is global to the player, so the case the entry names cannot be
represented at all, at any setting of the existing dials.

Both readings of the reflexive that the owner has kept live are *the same
mechanism at different cells of one table*, which is the reason this document
does not have to choose between them:

* one is `stance(herdedKind, herderKind) = PREY_OF_ME`
* the other is `stance(K, K) = PREY_OF_ME` for a herded kind `K`

One asymmetric table, two entries, neither privileged. If it later turns out
that only one cell does any work, that is a finding, not a decision taken here.

=== R2 — observed

Per animal, per tick. All of it is already computable inside `CACSystem`; no new
sensing infrastructure is required.

* the position and kind of every entity within `SENSE_RADIUS`
* any active `ActionState` whose expanding radius currently covers this animal,
  together with its `type` and the position of whatever emitted it

=== R3 — believed

State held in `CACBrainComponent`, persisting across ticks. This is the
difference between a reaction and a disposition: the animal carries it, rather
than the world recomputing it every frame.

`fear`:: as now, but raised *only* by an entity `E` where
`stance(self, E) = PREDATOR_OF_ME`. This single gate is the whole of the case
the entry names. A pressure act from anything else produces no fear at all — not
a reduced amount, none — however close and however loud.
`fearSource`:: which entity raised it. New, and required for correctness:
`FLEE` currently flees `pX, pZ` unconditionally (`src/systems.js:214-219`), so an
animal frightened by the Border Collie runs from the player instead. Neither
reading is observable until this is fixed.
`appetite`:: raised by proximity to an entity `E` where
`stance(self, E) = PREY_OF_ME`, scaled by a per-animal `appetiteBias` — a
sibling of the existing `fearBias` and `socialBias`. Decays when no such entity
is sensed.
`pursuing` + `pursuitHold`:: the entity this animal believes it is going after,
and how long that belief outlasts sensing it. This is what makes an appetitive
goal a distinct mechanism rather than pressure with the sign flipped, and it is
the thing the disengage test in step 5 actually tests.
`lureAffinity`:: which of the two attractor forms in R5 this animal answers to —
the herder's own body, a placed bait, or both. This is where the owner's ruling
that the difference between them matters is carried in state.

=== R4 — chosen, by the animal

Ordered and total, replacing the arbitration at `src/systems.js:199-209`. Two
implementations following this will agree.

. `fear > FEAR_FLEE` -> `FLEE`, vector away from `fearSource` — *not* from the
  player
. else `pursuing` is set and `appetite > APPETITE_PURSUE` -> `PURSUE`, vector
  toward `pursuing`
. else `curiosity > CURIOSITY_INVESTIGATE` -> `INVESTIGATE` (unchanged)
. else the role default (unchanged)

Note the ordering is unchanged in shape — aversion still outranks appetite. It
does not need to be re-ordered, because R3 stops the fear from ever being raised
in the cases this entry is about. That is the point: the gate is on the input,
not on the arbitration.

=== R5 — chosen, by the herder

* move (unchanged)
* emit a pressure act (unchanged) — which now simply *fails* against any animal
  for which the herder is not `PREDATOR_OF_ME`, with no special-casing anywhere
* *be* an attractor: the herder's own body, for any animal that treats the
  herder's kind as prey and whose `lureAffinity` admits it
* *place* an attractor: a bait entity with a kind of its own

=== R6 — the band, and what the two attractor forms cost

Displacement by an attractor succeeds while the range `r` between attractor and
animal is held inside `(R_STRIKE, R_INTEREST)` and the attractor moves toward
the pen.

* `r > R_INTEREST` — the animal stops sensing the attractor, `pursuitHold` runs
  down, and when it expires `pursuing` clears and the animal reverts to R4.4.
* `r < R_STRIKE` — the animal reaches the attractor.

The two forms fail differently, and this is where the owner's ruling has teeth:

* bait as attractor *fails safe* — a lost animal and a spent bait
* the herder as attractor *fails dangerous* — the thing arrives at the herder
* pressure also *fails safe* — the animal is simply not displaced

So the herder-as-attractor is the only one of the three with a cost at the near
edge of the band, and that cost is the only reason it would *play* differently
rather than merely look different. See D3.

One fact about the mockup that bears on this directly and is not a matter of
opinion: the player as hamster has `maxSpeed: 0.3` and the herd has
`maxSpeed: 0.5` (`src/main.js:93` and `src/main.js:103`). A pursuing animal is
faster than the herder it is pursuing, and the gain constants only affect
acceleration before the clamp — so it closes without fail. The near edge of the
band therefore *cannot* be held by running. It can only be held by something
else: terrain and the river, breaking sense range behind an obstacle, or
dropping a bait to reset `pursuing`. Whether that is interesting or merely
frustrating is exactly what D2 asks.

=== Constants

Named so that two implementations agree. The first three already exist in the
mockup at these values; the rest are proposed, and are deliberately mirrored on
the existing scales rather than invented fresh.

[cols="1,1,3"]
|===
|Name |Value |Note

|`SENSE_RADIUS` |30 |existing proximity radius, `src/systems.js:176`
|`FEAR_FLEE` |0.5 |existing, `src/systems.js:199`
|`CURIOSITY_INVESTIGATE` |0.4 |existing, `src/systems.js:201`
|`APPETITE_PURSUE` |0.4 |mirrors the curiosity threshold
|appetite rise |`dt * 0.5 * appetiteBias` |mirrors the fear rise
|appetite decay |`dt * 0.2` |mirrors the existing decay
|`PURSUIT_HOLD` |4.0 s |long enough to be visible in the step 5 test
|`R_INTEREST` |30 |same as `SENSE_RADIUS`, until there is reason to differ
|`R_STRIKE` |3.0 |just outside the 2.0 collision push, `src/systems.js:29`
|===

== Interim steps

The smallest thing that shows something. The mockup is disposable, so "fake it
in JS to see if the behaviour reads" is a legitimate first step and often the
right one. Steps, not a schedule.

Every one of these is a fake in the JS mockup, which is what the mockup is for.
Nothing below is a proposal to build anything in Rust.

Worth knowing before step 1, because it decides how cheap this is: *both verbs
already exist in the mockup, and one of them is already cancelled.* The lobby
defaults to "Hamster (Squeak Lure)" and "Cats (Curious, Skittish)"
(`index.html:43-50`); `PlayerInputSystem` gives the hamster `SQUEAK` and the
sheepdog `BARK` (`src/systems.js:302`); `SQUEAK` feeds `curiosity` and `BARK`
feeds `fear`. But the ungated proximity fear rises at `dt * 0.5 * 0.8` for a cat
(`fearBias: 0.8`, `src/main.js:108`), which is +0.4/s, crossing `FEAR_FLEE` in
about *1.25 seconds* — and `FLEE` is tested before `INVESTIGATE`. So a squeak
pulls a cat in for roughly a second, after which the ungated channel overrides
it and the cat leaves at three times the gain it approached with.

. *The negative demonstration, and it is the cheapest thing here.* Add `stance()`
  as a literal table and gate the proximity fear at `src/systems.js:176-178` on
  `PREDATOR_OF_ME`. Change nothing else — no appetite, no pursuit, no bait. On
  the lobby's existing default the cats should stop fleeing, and the squeak that
  is cancelled after ~1.25 s today should start holding. This shows the case the
  entry names *before any attractor code exists at all*. If it does not read as
  interesting on screen, this entry is in trouble already and D1 applies.
. *Flee the right thing.* Add `fearSource` and point the `FLEE` vector away from
  it instead of away from `pX, pZ`. Small, and required before either reading is
  observable — without it the Border Collie's bark still sends cats away from
  the player.
. *The second reading, in the same table, with no new code.* Set
  `stance(CAT, CAT) = PREY_OF_ME` and watch what a herd does when its members
  are each other's prey. This is the cheap way to find out whether that reading
  has content of its own or collapses into the other one.
. *The attractor proper, both forms.* Add `appetite`, `pursuing`, `pursuitHold`,
  the `PURSUE` goal, `R_INTEREST`/`R_STRIKE`, and a bait entity. Give some
  animals differing `lureAffinity` so both forms are visible in one run rather
  than in two.
. *The test that this is not pressure repainted.* Disengage — walk away fast. A
  real appetitive goal keeps the animal coming for `PURSUIT_HOLD` and then loses
  it; pressure with the sign flipped stops the instant the herder stops. The HUD
  already renders goal plus two bars (`src/main.js:174-189`); add `appetite` and
  `pursuing` to it. If the difference is invisible, the persistence is not doing
  work and should be cut — which is most of what distinguishes R3 from a tuned
  `socialBias`.
. *The near edge.* What happens at `R_STRIKE` when the attractor is the herder.
  Most discardable, most game-defining, and blocked on Q1.

== What would make us discard this

The owner's framing includes "potentially discard". An entry with no discard
condition has not been thought about yet.

Three, and the first is the real one. It is put first because it is the argument
*against* carrying this entry, and it is the strongest thing in this document.

=== D1 — if gating the fear is all it takes, this is already built

`fearBias` already exists per-animal (`src/components.js:40`). A cat spawned with
`fearBias: 0` and a raised `socialBias` would already ignore pressure and answer
squeaks — displacement by attraction rather than by pressure, in today's code,
with no new mechanism, no `stance` table and no R3. If that is the whole of it,
the honest conclusion is that this entry is *already implemented* and should be
closed as such rather than built.

Three things should survive that test. Run step 1, then check each one; if none
of them matters in play, drop the entry and just tune the biases.

* a scalar makes an animal ignore *everyone's* pressure, including the Border
  Collie's. The relation in R1 is per-pair; a bias is per-animal. Does that
  distinction ever show up on screen?
* a scalar gives no persistence after the herder disengages — no `pursuing`, no
  `PURSUIT_HOLD`, so nothing to see in step 5.
* a scalar gives no near edge to the band, therefore no cost, therefore no
  decision for the player.

=== D2 — if the band is not steerable, this is a chore and not a strategy

R6 establishes that the near edge cannot be held by running, because the pursuer
is faster than the herder. If holding `r` inside `(R_STRIKE, R_INTEREST)` *while
also choosing a direction* turns out to be either trivially easy or impossibly
fiddly with WASD and the existing camera modes, then there is no decision being
made and the entry does not earn its place. Discard it, or discard the band and
keep only the gate from step 1.

=== D3 — if the near edge has no cost, drop that half

Without a consequence at `R_STRIKE`, the herder-as-attractor is the
bait-as-attractor with extra steps, and the bait-as-attractor is pressure with
the sign flipped and a prop added. If the game does not want a fail state for
the herder, keep bait only — and then D1 has to be asked again, because a bait
that raises `curiosity` is expressible on the existing channel and may need
none of this.

== Open questions for the owner

. *What happens at `R_STRIKE` when the attractor is the herder?* This is the
  only unanswered thing that blocks work — step 6 cannot start without it, and
  D3 turns on it. Everything else in this document can proceed while it is open.
. *Is `stance` fixed when an animal spawns, or can it change with experience?*
  Asked rather than assumed. `trust` (`src/components.js:44`) is declared and is
  never read or written by any system in the mockup, and it has deliberately not
  been used anywhere above in case it is spoken for. Not proposing anything for
  it — just asking whether it is free.
. *Is `stance` keyed on kind, or may an individual differ from its kind?* R1 is
  written keyed on kind because that is cheaper. Keying it on the entity is not
  much harder, but it is a different table and worth deciding before it sets.
. *Under the second reading, does an animal that is prey to its own kind still
  flock?* The herd-centre average at `src/systems.js:116-125` currently means
  "where the herd is". If members are each other's prey it would have to mean
  something else, or nothing.
. *Naming.* `stance`, `appetite`, `pursuing`, `PURSUE`, `lureAffinity`,
  `R_INTEREST` and `R_STRIKE` are placeholders chosen to sit beside the existing
  vocabulary. Say so now if you want different ones, before they set.
